pathogen: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (bacterium spread by the Asian citrus psyllid)
summary: The most destructive citrus disease worldwide. An incurable bacterial infection spread by a small insect (psyllid) that leads to bitter, misshapen fruit and tree decline.
symptoms: Blotchy, asymmetric yellow mottling across leaf veins (unlike the symmetric pattern of nutrient deficiency)
Yellow shoots on part of the tree
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays partly green
Twig dieback and tree decline over a few years
key_sign: Blotchy yellow mottle that is not the same on both halves of the leaf.
favourable_conditions: Present wherever the Asian citrus psyllid is established; psyllids feed on new flush.
spread: Spread by the Asian citrus psyllid and by grafting infected budwood. There is no cure.

today: Look for psyllids on young flush (tiny insects sitting at a 45° angle, white waxy nymph secretions)
Inform your local agriculture or horticulture officer: HLB is a notifiable disease in many regions
this_week: Get the tree tested (PCR) to confirm
Begin psyllid control on all nearby citrus as advised by your officer
next_two_weeks: If confirmed and the tree is young or severely affected, remove it to protect neighbouring trees
Keep the remaining trees well fed and watered to slow decline

chemical: Insecticides labelled for Asian citrus psyllid (for example systemic neonicotinoids on young trees), applied as part of an area-wide programme; rotate modes of action
organic: Horticultural mineral oils and biological control of psyllids help reduce populations
cultural: Control psyllid host plants such as orange jessamine (Murraya paniculata) near the orchard

prevention: Plant only certified disease-free nursery trees
Coordinate psyllid control with neighbouring growers

sources.title: UF/IFAS: Florida Citrus Production Guide, Huanglongbing
